mainTopic: Why רבי אליעזר says a שור המועד must be slaughtered; the new פרק on doubtful damages and המוציא מחבירו עליו הראיה
overview: The amud opens with the last line of an earlier discussion: an ox that is fully מועד has no תם status left at all. The גמרא then asks why רבי אליעזר says a שור המועד can only be guarded with a knife. רבה learns it from ״וְלֹא יִשְׁמְרֶנּוּ״, but אביי shows that the same reading of ״וְלֹא יְכַסֶּנּוּ״ would mean a pit can never be covered, and a משנה says a properly covered pit makes the owner פטור. So אביי gives a new reason: you may not keep something dangerous in your house (״וְלֹא תָשִׂים דָּמִים בְּבֵיתֶךָ״). The פרק then ends, and a new משנה teaches cases where we don't know if a cow gave birth before or after a goring, so the calf's payment is cut to רביע נזק. שמואל says this split follows סומכוס, while the חכמים hold המוציא מחבירו עליו הראיה, even when one side is sure (ברי) and the other only says 'maybe' (שמא). The גמרא also connects the rule to the argument of רב and שמואל about an ox that was sold and turned out to gore. It narrows that case until nothing shows why the ox was bought. The discussion continues on the next amud.

steps.title: A fully forewarned ox has no innocent side left
steps.stepSummary: This closes an earlier discussion. An ox that is completely מועד keeps no part of its תם status.
steps.simpleTranslation: But an ox that is fully forewarned has no innocent side left at all.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes an earlier discussion by stating that a fully מועד ox keeps no part of its תם status.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before this line, the גמרא discussed an ox that is only partly מועד, so in some ways it is still treated as תם. This line sets that case against an ox that is completely מועד. For a fully מועד ox, nothing of the תם status remains.

keyTerms.meaning: A forewarned animal, one with an established habit of damaging, whose owner pays full damages
The status of being תם, an animal with no habit of damaging, whose owner pays only half damages

steps.whatToRemember: A completely מועד ox has no leftover תם status.

phrases.english: But an ox that is fully forewarned
you will not find in it
any innocent side at all.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: This is the closing line of a discussion that began before this section.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Once an ox is fully מועד, none of its תם status remains.

steps.title: Quoting רבי אליעזר in the משנה: only a knife works
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings back the words of רבי אליעזר in the משנה. He says the only safe way to guard a שור המועד is to slaughter it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אליעזר says: there is no way to guard it except with a knife.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes רבי אליעזר's words from the משנה to set up the next move, where it will look for his reason.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה, the חכמים discuss how well an owner must guard a dangerous ox to be exempt. רבי אליעזר takes the extreme view that no amount of guarding is enough for a מועד. Only slaughtering it truly protects the owner from paying.

keyTerms.meaning: Guarding, the safeguarding of a dangerous animal
A knife, meaning slaughtering the animal

phrases.english: Rabbi Eliezer says:
It has no guarding except a knife (etc.).
phrases.notes: The word in round brackets means 'and so on.' It points us back to the rest of the line in the משנה, and some versions leave it out.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר אוֹמֵר: אֵין לוֹ שְׁמִירָה אֶלָּא סַכִּין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: This starts a new topic by going back to the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבי אליעזר, a שור המועד can never be guarded well enough. Only slaughtering it truly protects the owner.

steps.title: רבה's source: "And he did not guard it"
steps.stepSummary: רבה explains that רבי אליעזר learns his rule from ״וְלֹא יִשְׁמְרֶנּוּ״. He reads it to mean that once an ox is מועד, no guarding is ever enough.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה said: What is רבי אליעזר's reason? The פסוק says "and he did not guard it." This means there is no longer any guarding for this ox.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה asks for the source of רבי אליעזר's view and answers it himself from a פסוק about the שור המועד.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבה does not read ״וְלֹא יִשְׁמְרֶנּוּ״ simply as 'the owner happened not to guard it.' He reads it as 'it cannot be guarded anymore.' On this reading the Torah is telling us that a מועד ox is beyond any normal guarding, so the owner pays unless it is slaughtered.
steps.confusionAlert: רבה is not saying the owner was simply careless. He reads the פסוק as saying this ox cannot be guarded at all anymore.

phrases.english: Rabba said:
What is the reason of Rabbi Eliezer?
Because the verse says: "and he did not guard it"
meaning there is no longer any guarding for this one.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבָּה: מַאי טַעְמָא דְּרַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source from the פסוק for רבי אליעזר's rule quoted in Step 2.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: ״וְלֹא יִשְׁמְרֶנּוּ״ teaches that a מועד ox can no longer be guarded at all.

steps.title: אביי: then a pit could never be covered either
steps.stepSummary: אביי challenges רבה by using the same reading on ״וְלֹא יְכַסֶּנּוּ״ by a בור. That would mean a pit can never be covered well enough.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to him: If so, the Torah also writes "and he did not cover it." Should that also mean there is no longer any covering for this pit?
steps.whatsHappening: אביי attacks רבה's reading by showing what it would do to a very similar פסוק about a pit.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two פסוקים are built the same way: ״וְלֹא יִשְׁמְרֶנּוּ״ for the ox and ״וְלֹא יְכַסֶּנּוּ״ for the pit. If רבה reads the first as 'it can never be guarded,' he would have to read the second as 'it can never be covered.' That second reading sounds very hard to accept.

keyTerms.meaning: If so, then from now on, an opening that pushes the other side's logic to a strange result
Covering, as in covering a pit

phrases.english: Abaye said to him:
If that is so,
what is written, "and he did not cover it," too
phrases.notes: שמות 21:33, the פסוק about someone who digs a pit and leaves it open.

phrases.english: does it mean there is no longer any covering for this one?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the way רבה read the פסוק in Step 3.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה's reading of ״וְלֹא יִשְׁמְרֶנּוּ״ as 'it can no longer be guarded'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The same reading applied to the matching פסוק ״וְלֹא יְכַסֶּנּוּ״ would mean a pit can never be covered properly.

steps.title: Blocking the reply: a משנה says a properly covered pit is exempt
steps.stepSummary: אביי heads off the answer 'yes, a pit really can't be covered.' He quotes a משנה that says a pit covered properly makes the owner פטור.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you say that is indeed true, didn't we learn: If he covered it properly, and an ox or a donkey fell in and died, he is exempt?
steps.whatsHappening: אביי closes off one way out for רבה by quoting a משנה. It proves that a pit can be covered well enough.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבה could have answered that even a covered pit makes its owner liable. אביי blocks this with a משנה: if the pit was covered properly and an animal still fell in, the owner is פטור. So covering a pit does work, and the reading 'no covering is ever enough' must be wrong. By the same logic, רבה's reading of ״וְלֹא יִשְׁמְרֶנּוּ״ is now in trouble.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you would say, 'yes, that is so'
But didn't we learn in a משנה?

steps.whyThisMatters: Reading ״וְלֹא יְכַסֶּנּוּ״ as 'a pit can never be covered' contradicts a משנה. Since רבה read the matching words ״וְלֹא יִשְׁמְרֶנּוּ״ the same way, his source for רבי אליעזר is now in doubt.

phrases.english: And if you would say that indeed it is so,
but didn't we learn in a mishna:
If he covered it properly,

phrases.aramaic: וְנָפַל לְתוֹכוֹ שׁוֹר אוֹ חֲמוֹר וּמֵת –
phrases.english: and an ox or a donkey fell into it and died
he is exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes אביי's challenge from Step 4 by blocking the answer 'yes, a pit can't be covered.'
steps.kashyaTarget: The possible reply that a pit indeed can never be covered well enough
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A משנה rules that a pit covered properly makes the owner פטור. So covering does work, and the matching reading of ״וְלֹא יִשְׁמְרֶנּוּ״ falls apart.

steps.title: אביי gives a new reason: do not keep danger in your house
steps.stepSummary: אביי drops רבה's reading. He explains that רבי אליעזר's rule comes from רבי נתן's teaching that a person may not keep a dangerous dog or a shaky ladder in his house, as the פסוק says ״וְלֹא תָשִׂים דָּמִים בְּבֵיתֶךָ״.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, אביי said: This is רבי אליעזר's reason. As a ברייתא teaches, רבי נתן says: How do we know that a person may not raise a vicious dog in his house, and may not set up a shaky ladder in his house? Because the פסוק says, 'You shall not bring blood into your house.'
steps.whatsHappening: אביי gives up on רבה's explanation and offers a new reason why רבי אליעזר says a שור המועד must be slaughtered.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבה read ״וְלֹא יִשְׁמְרֶנּוּ״ as 'no guarding ever helps,' but that same reading would wreck the בור case, as we saw in steps 4-5. אביי moves the source to a different idea: a person may not keep something dangerous in his home at all. A שור המועד is like a vicious dog, so the safe thing is to get rid of it, and that is why רבי אליעזר says to slaughter it.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather. It signals that the earlier explanation is dropped and a new one is coming.
As it is taught in a ברייתא
Do not bring blood into your house. The source for not keeping dangers at home.

steps.whatToRemember: According to אביי, רבי אליעזר's rule is not about guarding being useless. It is about the איסור of keeping a dangerous thing in your home.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that רבי אליעזר's demand to slaughter the ox may come from a general איסור against keeping danger around. It is not only a rule about how to guard a damaging animal.

phrases.english: Rather, Abaye said:
This is the reason of Rabbi Eliezer:
phrases.notes: He means רבי אליעזר's rule from the משנה that the only safe guarding for a מועד ox is the knife.

phrases.english: As it is taught: Rabbi Natan says:
From where do we know that a person may not raise
a vicious dog inside his house,

phrases.aramaic: וְאַל יַעֲמִיד סוּלָּם רָעוּעַ בְּתוֹךְ בֵּיתוֹ?
phrases.english: and may not set up a shaky ladder inside his house?
As it is stated: "You shall not bring blood into your house."

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אָמַר אַבָּיֵי: הַיְינוּ טַעְמֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces רבה's source after אביי's challenges from the בור case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Replacing the source: a new פסוק gives the reason, so the problem with רבה's reading no longer matters.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי אליעזר learns from ״וְלֹא יִשְׁמְרֶנּוּ״ that no guarding ever helps. That reading would also make a covered pit useless.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי אליעזר's reason is the איסור of keeping a danger at home (״וְלֹא תָשִׂים דָּמִים בְּבֵיתֶךָ״). So the מועד ox should be slaughtered.

steps.title: Hadran — Closing the chapter of an ox that gored four or five times
steps.stepSummary: The closing formula for the end of the פרק שור שנגח ארבעה וחמשה.
steps.simpleTranslation: We will return to you, chapter 'An ox that gored four or five times.'
steps.whatsHappening: The פרק is finished. This is the standard line said at the end of a chapter.
steps.deeperAnalysis: No new הלכה is added here. It only marks that the discussion of this פרק has ended and a new פרק is about to begin.

keyTerms.meaning: We will return to you. Said when finishing a פרק.

phrases.english: We will return to you,
"An ox that gored four or five"
phrases.notes: This is the name of the chapter, taken from its opening words.

steps.triggerLanguage: הֲדַרַן עֲלָךְ שׁוֹר שֶׁנָּגַח אַרְבָּעָה וַחֲמִשָּׁה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the פרק after אביי's final explanation.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The פרק שור שנגח ארבעה וחמשה is complete.

steps.title: An ox gores a cow and her calf is found next to her
steps.stepSummary: An ox gored a pregnant cow and a dead calf is found beside her. Nobody knows if she gave birth before or after the goring. The owner pays half damages for the cow and quarter damages for the calf.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: An ox gored a cow, and the cow's fetus was found next to her. It is not known whether she gave birth before the goring or after it. The ox's owner pays half damages for the cow and a quarter damages for the calf.
steps.whatsHappening: A new פרק opens with a משנה about a doubtful case: we do not know if the goring caused the calf's death.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For the cow, the owner pays the usual חצי נזק of a תם ox. For the calf there is a doubt: if she gave birth before the goring, the ox did not hurt the calf, and if after, it did. Because of the doubt, he pays half of the half, which is רביע נזק.

keyTerms.meaning: Half the damage. What the owner of a תם ox pays.
An ox that has not yet been warned. Its owner pays half.

phrases.english: MISHNA: An ox that gored a cow
and her fetus was found at her side,
and it is not known
whether she gave birth before it gored her,
or whether she gave birth after it gored her —
he pays half damages for the cow,
and quarter damages for the offspring.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִי׳ שׁוֹר שֶׁנָּגַח אֶת הַפָּרָה וְנִמְצָא עוּבָּרָהּ בְּצִדָּהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new פרק and a new topic.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When it is not known if the goring caused the calf's loss, the owner pays full חצי נזק for the cow and only רביע נזק for the calf.

steps.title: A cow gores an ox and her calf is found next to her
steps.stepSummary: The reverse case: a cow gored an ox and her calf is found beside her. Nobody knows if the calf was born before or after she gored. Half damages are collected from the cow and a quarter from the calf.
steps.simpleTranslation: And likewise, a cow gored an ox, and her calf was found next to her. It is not known whether she gave birth before she gored or after. Half damages are collected from the cow, and a quarter damages from the calf.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives a second case with the same doubt, but now the cow is the one doing the damage.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A תם pays only from the body of the animal that did the damage, so the money is taken from the cow. If the calf was still inside her when she gored, it counts as part of her and can be collected from. Since we don't know, only half of that amount, a quarter of the damage, can be taken from the calf.

keyTerms.meaning: Is collected. Payment is taken from this animal.
And likewise. The same rule works in this case too.

steps.confusionAlert: Watch the switch in wording. In the first case it says מְשַׁלֵּם, 'he pays FOR' the cow and calf, because they are the victims. Here it says מִשְׁתַּלֵּם, 'it is collected FROM' the cow and calf, because the cow did the damage.
steps.whatToRemember: In both cases of the משנה, the doubt about the calf cuts its amount in half: רביע נזק instead of חצי נזק.

phrases.english: And likewise, a cow that gored an ox
and her offspring was found at her side,
and it is not known
whether she gave birth before she gored,
or whether she gave birth after she gored —
half damages are collected from the cow,
and quarter damages from the offspring.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכֵן פָּרָה שֶׁנָּגְחָה אֶת הַשּׁוֹר וְנִמְצָא וְלָדָהּ בְּצִדָּהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the same doubt rule to the reverse case, where the cow is the one that damaged.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When a cow gores and it is unknown if her calf was born before the goring, חצי נזק is collected from the cow and רביע נזק from the calf.

steps.title: The משנה follows סומכוס; the חכמים say the one taking money must prove
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה in the name of שמואל says the משנה's ruling of splitting the damages follows סומכוס. The חכמים disagree and say that whoever wants to take money from his fellow must bring proof.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: רב יהודה said in the name of שמואל: This is the view of סומכוס, who says that money in doubt is split. But the חכמים say: This is a great rule in law: whoever wants to take money from his fellow must bring the proof.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins explaining the משנה. It tells us whose opinion the 'split the payment' ruling follows, and that the חכמים hold differently.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה, nobody knew whether the calf was born before or after the goring, so the payment was split. שמואל says that splitting a doubt is סומכוס's view. The חכמים say that when there is a doubt, the one who wants to take money from someone else gets nothing unless he brings proof.

keyTerms.meaning: A תנא who holds that money in doubt is divided
Money whose owner is in doubt
The one who wants to take money from his fellow must bring proof
A great rule in monetary law

steps.whyThisMatters: 'המוציא מחבירו עליו הראיה' is one of the most basic rules of money cases across all of ש״ס.

phrases.english: גמרא:
Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel:
This is the view of Sumchus,
phrases.notes: 'This' is the משנה we just learned, where the payment for the calf was split because of the doubt.

phrases.english: who says: money in doubt is divided.
But the Sages say:
This is a great rule in law:
the one who takes money from his fellow must bring the proof.

steps.triggerLanguage: אמר רב יהודה אמר שמואל זו דברי סומכוס
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains whose opinion the משנה in steps 8-9 follows.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The משנה follows סומכוס (split the doubt); the חכמים hold המוציא מחבירו עליו הראיה.

steps.title: Why add the words 'this is a great rule'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the חכמים needed to say 'זה כלל גדול בדין' instead of just stating the rule.
steps.simpleTranslation: Why do I need them to say 'This is a great rule in law'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks about the extra words the חכמים used. This sets up the next step, which explains what those words add.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule itself could have been stated plainly. Calling it a 'great rule' suggests it covers more cases than the obvious one, so the גמרא wants to know which ones.

keyTerms.meaning: Why do I need to say it?

phrases.english: Why do I need to say
'This is a great rule in law'?

steps.triggerLanguage: למה לי למימר זה כלל גדול בדין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the wording of the חכמים quoted in step 10.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the extra phrase 'זה כלל גדול בדין' comes to teach.

steps.title: Even a certain claim against an unsure defendant needs proof
steps.stepSummary: The words are needed to teach that even when the injured party is certain and the damager is only unsure, the one taking money still must bring proof.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was needed, because even if the injured party says 'I am sure' and the damager says 'maybe,' the one who wants to take money from his fellow must bring proof.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question: the 'great rule' applies even in a case where you might have thought the claimant wins.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One might think a sure claim ('ברי') beats an unsure answer ('שמא'). The phrase 'great rule' teaches that this is not enough. Without proof, the money stays with the one who has it.

keyTerms.meaning: The injured party / the one who caused the damage

steps.confusionAlert: Don't assume 'בָּרִי' always wins over 'שֶׁמָּא.' Here the חכמים say even a sure claim cannot take money without proof.

phrases.english: It was needed,
because even if the injured party says 'I am certain,'
and the damager says 'maybe,'
the one who takes from his fellow must bring the proof.

steps.triggerLanguage: אצטריך דאפילו ניזק אומר ברי ומזיק אומר שמא
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The phrase extends the rule even to a case of ברי against שמא.

steps.title: Another answer: the ox sold and found to be a gorer
steps.stepSummary: A second answer: the phrase covers a case like the ox that was sold and turned out to gore. רב says the sale was a mistake; שמואל says the seller can claim he sold it for slaughter.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or else, it teaches a case like this one that was said: If someone sells an ox to his friend and it turns out to be a gorer, רב says it is a mistaken sale. שמואל says the seller can tell him, 'I sold it to you for slaughter.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second answer for why the חכמים said 'great rule,' by bringing a case where רב and שמואל argue.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A goring ox is no good for work but fine for slaughter. רב says the buyer can cancel the sale. שמואל says the seller can claim it was sold for slaughter, so the buyer, who wants his money back, cannot get it without proof. That fits the 'great rule' of the חכמים.

keyTerms.meaning: A mistaken sale, which can be cancelled

phrases.english: Alternatively, for a case like this that was said:
One who sells an ox to his fellow,
and it turns out to be a gorer:

phrases.aramaic: רַב אָמַר: הֲרֵי זֶה מִקָּח טָעוּת.
phrases.english: Rav says: this is a mistaken sale.
And Shmuel says: he can say to him,
'I sold it to you for slaughter.'

steps.triggerLanguage: אי נמי לכי הא דאתמר המוכר שור לחבירו ונמצא נגחן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second answer to the question of step 11.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The phrase covers cases like the goring ox, where שמואל leaves the money with the seller unless the buyer proves otherwise.

steps.title: Why not just look at what kind of buyer he is?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the argument: why guess? Just check whether this buyer usually buys oxen for plowing or for slaughter.
steps.simpleTranslation: Why? Let us see whether he is a man who buys for plowing, or a man who buys for slaughter!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the case of the goring ox: the doubt seems easy to solve by looking at the buyer's usual habits.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the buyer is known as a farmer, he clearly bought it for work. If he is a butcher, he clearly bought it for meat. So why would רב and שמואל need to argue about it?

phrases.english: Why?
Let us see whether he is a man who buys for plowing,
or a man who buys for slaughter!

steps.triggerLanguage: אמאי וניחזי אי גברא דזבין לרדיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the case brought in step 13.
steps.kashyaTarget: The argument of רב and שמואל about the goring ox.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The buyer's known habits should settle why he bought it, so there is no real doubt to argue about.

steps.title: The buyer buys for both purposes
steps.stepSummary: The argument is about a buyer who buys oxen both for plowing and for slaughter, so his habits don't settle the question.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it is needed for a man who buys for this and for that.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the case is about a buyer whose habits could go either way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the buyer sometimes buys for work and sometimes for meat, looking at him tells us nothing. So the doubt is real, and רב and שמואל can argue about it.

keyTerms.meaning: It is only needed for a case where...

phrases.english: No, it is needed
for a man who buys for this and for that.

steps.triggerLanguage: לא צריכא בגברא דזבין להא ולהא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The buyer's usual habits should show why he bought the ox.
steps.terutzMaskana: The case is about a buyer who buys for both purposes, so the doubt remains.

steps.title: Why not check the price that was paid?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests another way to settle the question: if the buyer paid the price of a plowing ox, it was for plowing; if he paid the price of a meat ox, it was for slaughter.
steps.simpleTranslation: But let us look at the price. If he paid the price of a plowing ox, it was for plowing. If he paid the price of a slaughter ox, it was for slaughter!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the case again. Even if the buyer's habits don't tell us anything, the price he paid should show what he was buying.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 15 said the buyer buys both kinds of oxen, so his habits can't decide the case. Now the גמרא points to another clue: plowing oxen and meat oxen usually sell for different prices. If the price settles the question, there is nothing left for רב and שמואל to argue about.

keyTerms.meaning: Slaughter (an ox bought for its meat)

phrases.english: But let us look and see
if it was the price of a plowing ox, it was for plowing;
if it was the price of a slaughter ox, it was for slaughter!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of step 15 with a new clue: the price paid.
steps.kashyaTarget: The case of the argument between רב and שמואל as defined in step 15
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The price paid shows the purpose of the sale, so there should be no doubt and no argument.

steps.title: Meat prices went up, so the price proves nothing
steps.stepSummary: The argument is about a time when meat became expensive, so a slaughter ox cost the same as a plowing ox. The price cannot show what the buyer intended.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, the argument is needed for a case where meat became expensive, and a slaughter ox costs the same as a plowing ox.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers step 16. It narrows the case to a time when both kinds of oxen sold for the same price.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Usually the price tells us what kind of ox was bought. But when meat prices rise, a meat ox becomes as costly as a plowing ox. Then the price gives no clue, the doubt stays, and רב and שמואל can really argue about who must bring proof.

keyTerms.meaning: It is needed only for this case (the argument is about a specific situation)

steps.whatToRemember: The argument between רב and שמואל is limited to a case where nothing (not the buyer's habits and not the price) shows why the ox was bought. Only then does the question of who must bring proof matter.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows the גמרא working to keep the case a real doubt. That way, the rule from the earlier steps, that the one taking money must bring proof, really applies here.

phrases.english: No, it is needed
where meat became expensive,
and it stands at the price of a plowing ox.
phrases.notes: 'It' is the ox bought for meat. Its price rose until it matched a plowing ox.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case (אוקימתא): a situation where the prices were the same
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The price paid would show whether the ox was bought for plowing or for slaughter.
steps.terutzMaskana: When meat prices rose to equal plowing-ox prices, the price shows nothing, so the doubt remains.

steps.title: The גמרא begins a new response
steps.stepSummary: The word 'אמרי' ('they said') opens the next response in the discussion. That response continues on the next amud.
steps.whatsHappening: This is only a setup line. The גמרא is getting ready for its next move, which comes right after this word.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'אמרי' ('they say') is the usual way the גמרא brings an anonymous response. It isn't the חכמים of the משנה. The content comes on the next amud, so here it only marks that a new response is beginning.

keyTerms.meaning: They say (the גמרא's usual way to bring an anonymous response)

steps.confusionAlert: Don't look for a ruling in this line. It is only the opening word of the next statement.

phrases.english: They said:

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the next response after the answer in step 17.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Setup only; the content of the statement comes on the next amud.
